clue.text: On rising, very old person (male not female) not at all stiff

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means the built word is read from the bottom up, so backwards
'male not female' tells us to put the male letter where the female one was

parts.note: an old fogey is jokingly called a fossil

explanation.surface: An ancient man, rising from his seat, turns out to be surprisingly supple.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping F for M in FOSSIL gives MOSSIL; 'rising' turns that upwards to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Lissom describes a body that is supple and lithe, the opposite of rigid.

clue.text: Ferrari — one's overturned round bend

indicators.note: round says the reversed word wraps around the next piece
in a down clue, overturned means the word is flipped so it reads backwards

parts.note: the number one written as a word; the 's is a link meaning 'is'
the letter Z is shaped like a zigzag bend, as on a road sign

explanation.surface: A Ferrari car flips over while taking a sharp corner.
explanation.walkthrough: Turning ONE gives ENO; 'round' puts Z inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Enzo was the first name of the founder of the Italian motor company Ferrari.

clue.text: Girl portrayed female TV personality on radio

indicators.note: something heard on the radio is only heard, so the words are judged by their sound

parts.note: portrayed means drew, and Cilla Black was a famous British female TV presenter

explanation.surface: A young woman was depicted as a female TV star in a radio broadcast.
explanation.walkthrough: Cilla Black was a Liverpool singer who presented popular British TV shows such as Blind Date; DREW CILLA said aloud sounds like the girl's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Drusilla is a female given name, Roman in origin, so it names a girl.

clue.text: Largely shaking up a family code

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the shortened word is read from the bottom up
largely means most of the word is used, so its last letter goes

parts.note: a tremor is a shaking or quiver

explanation.surface: Something largely shakes up the rules a household lives by.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shaking' looks like an anagram signal but is a noun; 'Largely' drops its last letter and 'up' turns what is left before A is added. OMERTA is a single word, not 'Largely' fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Omertà is the Mafia's vow of silence, the code of conduct of a crime family.

clue.text: Newborn babies get one slap on buttocks

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means the first piece sits on top of the next
slap suggests something done carelessly, as in slapdash, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: nates is the anatomical word for buttocks

explanation.surface: A midwife gives each new arrival the traditional slap on the bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slap' rearranges ONE to NEO, placed 'on' NATES, the Latin-derived anatomical term for the buttocks.
explanation.definitionFit: Neonates are infants in their first weeks of life, the medical term for the newly born.

clue.text: Have to stop boy making such a motion

indicators.note: to stop means to plug a gap, so one piece is put inside the other

parts.note: Brian is a boy's name
to have something is to own it

explanation.surface: A boy is told to halt, which creates a certain movement.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is adjectival in force: Brownian names the motion, as in 'Brownian motion', the random jiggling of particles in a fluid.
explanation.definitionFit: Brownian motion is the random movement of small particles suspended in a liquid or gas, named after botanist Robert Brown.

clue.text: Stewart Murray accepted as name of author

indicators.note: accepted means one piece takes the other inside it

parts.note: Rod Stewart is a British rock singer
Al Murray is a British comedian known as the Pub Landlord

explanation.surface: Two celebrities agree on what to call a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Rod Stewart is a famous British rock singer and Al Murray a British stand-up comedian; the surface reads them as surnames.
explanation.definitionFit: Roald Dahl wrote Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, so Roald is a writer's first name.

clue.text: Almost unable to bear commoners?

indicators.note: almost means the word is cut short by its final letter

parts.note: without a womb, a woman cannot bear children

explanation.surface: Ordinary folk almost can't stand it.
explanation.walkthrough: The Wombles are furry creatures from British children's books and TV who live on Wimbledon Common, hence 'commoners' with its question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: The Wombles live beneath Wimbledon Common, so they are punningly residents of a common.

clue.text: Rhea about to bite mate from abroad

indicators.note: to bite means one piece closes its teeth around the other

parts.note: re is Latin for about, concerning
ami is French for friend

explanation.surface: A large flightless bird is about to peck a foreign friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rhea' looks like the ostrich-like bird but is the plant: rhea is another name for ramie.
explanation.definitionFit: Ramie, also called rhea or China grass, is a nettle-family plant grown for fibre.

clue.text: Mike's plan lame

parts.note: Mike is the radio code word for the letter M
an aim is a plan or intention

explanation.surface: Mike's scheme is feeble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lame' looks like an adjective but is the verb to lame, to cripple.
explanation.definitionFit: To lame someone is to cripple or disable them, the same as wounding badly.

clue.text: Original sin — one's right about Eve's part

indicators.note: original means the first, so only the opening letter of sin is taken
about suggests the letters are moved around into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Adam is told he was right about Eve's role in the first sin of Eden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eve' looks like Adam's partner but is actor Trevor Eve, who played the radio-phone-in private detective Eddie Shoestring in the BBC TV series Shoestring (1979-80); 'about' rearranges S, ONES and RIGHT.
explanation.definitionFit: Trevor Eve's best-known television role was the title detective in the BBC series Shoestring.

clue.text: Somebody admired united's head of marketing? That's a fallacy

parts.note: an idol is someone admired or adored
U is the abbreviation for united, as in football club names

indicators.note: head of means the first letter of the following word

explanation.surface: A football club's star turns out to be a marketing myth.
explanation.walkthrough: IDOLUM is a philosophical term for a false notion; 'That's' points back to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: An idolum is a mistaken idea or false mental image, an error of reasoning.

clue.text: Label can't offer contracts for this type of singing

indicators.note: the words contract, holding the answer inside them

explanation.surface: A record company cannot offer deals for operatic vocalists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'contracts' seems to be record deals but signals that the answer is held inside 'Label can't offer'.
explanation.definitionFit: Bel canto is the lyrical Italian operatic style of singing with smooth, beautiful tone.

clue.text: Batted feebly and left out? Not this guy

indicators.note: batted suggests the letters are knocked about into a new order
out means the named letter is removed

explanation.surface: A cricketer who batted weakly and was dropped could never be a famous big hitter.
explanation.walkthrough: BEEFY was the nickname of Ian Botham, the England cricket all-rounder known for aggressive batting, so he is the guy who never batted feebly.
explanation.definitionFit: Beefy is the nickname of English cricketer Ian Botham, a hard-hitting batsman.

clue.text: What setter set is difficult -try to assess reaction

indicators.note: is difficult suggests the letters are in a tricky tangle needing rearrangement

explanation.surface: The crossword compiler's puzzle is hard, so solvers probe how others respond.
explanation.walkthrough: All thirteen letters of 'What setter set' rearrange to give the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: To test the waters is an idiom for gauging opinion cautiously before acting.

clue.text: Rated as compromise

parts.note: the clue word is what you get when the word for commerce is taken off (shuffled), so the wordplay reads backwards from it

explanation.surface: Something was judged to be a happy middle ground.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: OFF is an anagram signal, so TRADE OFF would be a clue for RATED; 'as' links.
explanation.definitionFit: A trade-off is a balance struck between competing aims, giving up one to gain another.

clue.text: Set record making ski turn

parts.note: a television set is informally a telly or tele
to mark is to record, as in marking a score

explanation.surface: Someone sets a record by performing a skiing manoeuvre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set record' reads as achieving a best, but 'Set' is a television set.
explanation.definitionFit: A telemark is a skiing turn made with one ski advanced and the knee bent, from Norway.

clue.text: Man and wife gutted about book — a treasured possession

indicators.note: about means the pieces before it are turned round to read backwards

parts.note: a male is a man

indicators.note: gutted means the insides are removed, leaving the first and last letters

explanation.surface: A married couple are devastated over a book that meant everything to them.
explanation.walkthrough: MALE and WE (wife without its middle) turned 'about' give EWELAM, then B; the phrase comes from Nathan's parable in the Bible of a poor man's one beloved lamb.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Bible, a poor man's only ewe lamb is his single cherished thing, hence the idiom.

clue.text: Station Wood back outside state line

indicators.note: outside means the reversed word goes around the other pieces
back means the word is read in reverse

parts.note: yew is a wood, from the yew tree
to aver is to state firmly

explanation.surface: A railway terminal called Wood sits behind a state boundary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wood' looks like a forest but is a tree's timber, turned 'back' to wrap round the rest. Waverley is Edinburgh's main railway station.
explanation.definitionFit: Edinburgh Waverley is the main railway terminus in Scotland's capital.

clue.text: Ridge climbing round north shows guts

indicators.note: round means the reversed word wraps around the letter that follows
in a down clue, climbing means the word goes upward, so reads backwards

parts.note: an arete is a sharp mountain ridge

explanation.surface: A mountain ridge being scaled near the north tests the climbers' nerve.
explanation.walkthrough: ARETE climbing becomes ETERA, then 'round' puts N inside it after the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Entera is the plural of enteron, the alimentary canal, so it means the intestines.

clue.text: Power in beginning shown by old car indicator

indicators.note: in means the power letter goes inside the word for beginning

parts.note: a seed is the beginning from which something grows
P is the physics symbol for power

explanation.surface: A vintage car's dial shows power from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Speedo' is the British short form of speedometer.
explanation.definitionFit: A speedometer, shortened colloquially, is the dashboard gauge showing a vehicle's rate.

clue.text: Copper briefly said goodbye

indicators.note: said means the letters are spoken rather than read

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper, a brief form

explanation.surface: A police officer quickly bade farewell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' looks like a policeman but is the element, whose symbol CU spoken as letters gives a farewell.
explanation.definitionFit: See you is a casual parting phrase, a way to bid farewell.

clue.text: Live shows turning blue (with a bit of luck)

indicators.note: turning means the word is turned round to read backwards

parts.note: blue means risque or lewd

indicators.note: a bit of means just the opening letter is taken

explanation.surface: A show performed live is turning racy, with a little good fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blue' means smutty here, not sad or the colour; 'shows' and 'with' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: To dwell somewhere is to reside, to make one's home there.

clue.text: Rugby player takes issue over measure

indicators.note: takes means the first piece holds the second inside it

parts.note: a centre is a rugby back position

indicators.note: over means the word is turned over to read backwards

parts.note: to emit is to issue

explanation.surface: A rugby player disputes a tackle over a judgement call.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes issue' reads as disagreeing, but 'takes' is the container signal and 'issue' is a verb turned 'over'. A centre is one of the rugby backs.
explanation.definitionFit: A centimetre is a unit of length, a hundredth of a metre.

clue.text: Upset about rubbish band

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means both pieces are turned upside down, reading backwards

parts.note: C stands for circa, Latin for about
rot is nonsense, rubbish

explanation.surface: Someone is upset about a terrible music group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'band' looks like a pop group but is a neck ring.
explanation.definitionFit: A torc is a metal neck ring worn by ancient Celts, a rigid band of twisted gold.

clue.text: Former president (Richard) conclusively lying here

parts.note: Abe is Abraham Lincoln, a former US president

indicators.note: conclusively means only the final letter is used

explanation.surface: A past president, Richard Nixon perhaps, finally stretched out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Richard' tempts toward Nixon as the president, but only its last letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Abed means in bed, the place where one is reclining.

clue.text: One shooting father out of anger

indicators.note: out of means the father letters lie outside the word for anger

parts.note: Fr is the abbreviation for father, a priest
ire is anger

explanation.surface: A man fires a gun because his father is angry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of anger' reads as a motive, but places FR outside IRE.
explanation.definitionFit: A firer is a person who discharges a gun, a shooter.

clue.text: Take lead from what you can see at chelsea, mass of soil round plant

parts.note: R is short for recipe, Latin for take, on prescriptions

indicators.note: lead from means the opening letter is taken away

parts.words: what you can see at chelsea
parts.note: Chelsea is a London football club, so football is what is seen there

explanation.surface: A gardener replants a shrub with its earth intact, near Chelsea's stadium.
explanation.walkthrough: Chelsea is a London football club; R replaces the first letter of FOOTBALL.
explanation.definitionFit: A rootball is the compact mass of roots and earth lifted with a plant for transplanting.
